title: Flood fill without recursion
description:
Write `floodFill(map, x, y)`. It floods the region of `'.'` cells connected to the cell at column `x`, row `y`, changing each one to `'~'`, and returns how many cells it changed. Cells connect up, down, left and right, not diagonally. Any other character is a wall.

If the starting cell is outside the map or is not `'.'`, nothing changes and the result is 0.

The function must not call itself. Keep the cells still to visit in a `std::vector` used as a stack, so the program's own stack stays small however big the map is.

```
#######        #######
#..#..#        #~~#..#
#..#..#   ->   #~~#..#      floodFill(map, 1, 1) returns 4
####..#        ####..#
#######        #######
```
hints: A `std::pair<int, int>` (from `<utility>`) is two values in one object. `toVisit.push_back({ x, y });` adds a cell, and for a pair `p`, `p.first` is the column and `p.second` the row.
Push the starting cell, then loop while the vector is not empty. Each time round, take the last cell off with `back()` and `pop_back()`.
Check the cell when you take it off, not when you push it: if it is outside the map or not `'.'`, skip it with `continue`.
Otherwise mark it `'~'`, count it, and push its four neighbours. Some of them will be walls or already flooded; the check at the top of the loop deals with those.
rules: Do not call floodFill from inside itself: use the vector of cells to visit instead.
lessonTitle: The Stack: Frames, Locals and Return Addresses
